title: Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data?
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
harvard_reference: Grinsztajn, L., Oyallon, E. and Varoquaux, G. (2022) 'Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data?', in Koyejo, S., Mohamed, S., Agarwal, A., Belgrave, D., Cho, K. and Oh, A. (eds) Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022), Datasets and Benchmarks Track. New Orleans, LA, 28 November-9 December 2022. Curran Associates, pp. 507-520. doi:10.52202/068431-0037.
abstract_summary: The authors ask whether deep learning's dominance on text and images carries over to tabular data. They assemble a benchmark of 45 tabular datasets from varied domains and a methodology that accounts for both model fitting and hyperparameter search (about 20,000 compute hours of random search per learner), comparing tree-based ensembles (RandomForest, GradientBoostingTree, XGBoost) against standard and tabular-specific neural networks (MLP, ResNet, FT-Transformer, SAINT). On medium-sized data (training sets truncated to ~10K samples) tree-based models remain state of the art even before accounting for their speed advantage, and the gap persists across every random-search budget rather than closing after tuning. Section 5 investigates inductive biases and reports three findings: neural networks are biased towards overly smooth solutions while the target functions in these datasets are irregular; uninformative features hurt MLP-like networks far more than trees; and tabular data are not rotation-invariant, so rotation-invariant architectures discard a natural feature basis. The paper also releases the benchmark and all raw search results.

claims_supported.claim: On medium-sized tabular datasets, tree-based ensembles (random forests, gradient boosting) remain state of the art and outperform deep learning, even after tuning, partly because neural networks are biased towards smooth functions and are hurt by uninformative features.
claims_supported.where: Abstract: tree-based models (XGBoost, Random Forests) remain state-of-the-art on medium-sized data (~10K samples) even without accounting for their superior speed; and the three challenges for tabular NNs include being robust to uninformative features and being able to learn irregular functions. Section 4.2 (benchmark results): "Tree-based models are superior for every random search budget" and the gap stays wide even after many random-search iterations, i.e. it does not disappear after hyperparameter tuning. Section 5.2, Finding 1: neural networks are biased to overly smooth solutions, and the target functions in the benchmark datasets are irregular, which NNs struggle to fit compared with tree-based models (linked to the spectral bias towards low-frequency functions). Section 5.3, Finding 2: uninformative features affect MLP-like NNs more than tree-based models; removing them narrows the gap and adding them widens it. Every component of the claim (medium-sized regime, RF and GBT as the tree models, persistence after tuning, smoothness bias, sensitivity to uninformative features) is made explicitly in the paper.

caveats: The paper defines 'medium-sized' as training sets truncated to 10,000 samples (with a separate large-sized benchmark of 50,000); the Telco Customer Churn dataset (~7,043 rows before splitting) is smaller than that regime, so the report should present the finding as the closest available evidence rather than a direct benchmark of Telco-scale data. The result is for 2022-era architectures (MLP, ResNet, FT-Transformer, SAINT); the report should not imply the paper evaluated later tabular foundation models. 'Even after tuning' refers to the paper's random-search hyperparameter budgets, not to every possible tuning strategy. The paper's third finding (non-rotation-invariance of tabular data) is an additional reason for the gap that the candidate claim does not mention; 'partly because' is therefore appropriate wording.
